subject: general
question: Which of the following accurately describes the legal and institutional basis of "Special Category State" status in India?

options.text: It is a constitutional provision granted under Article 275.
It is defined in the Constitution and recommended by the Inter-State Council.
It is not mentioned in the Constitution and was granted by the National Development Council.
It is conferred by the Finance Commission under Article 280.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It is not mentioned in the Constitution and was granted by the National Development Council.**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The status of **Special Category State (SCS)** in India is **not a constitutional provision**. It is an administrative classification introduced by the **National Development Council (NDC)** in 1969. 
• The NDC granted this status to states that faced challenges such as **hilly terrain**, **low population density**, **strategic location** (bordering neighboring countries), **economic backwardness**, or **non-viable nature of state finances**. 
• States with SCS status receive **preferential treatment** in the allocation of central funds and other financial assistance, particularly under the Gadgil-Mukherjee formula for central assistance. 
• **Originally, the SCS status** was conferred to **Assam, Nagaland, Jammu & Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh**. Over time, more states were added to the list, bringing the total to **11** states. 
• The **14th Finance Commission** (2015) recommended doing away with the distinction between SCS and other states. However, some benefits are still provided to SCS states through other mechanisms. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Criteria for Special Category States:** 
• **Hilly terrain:** States with challenging geographical conditions, such as the northeastern states and Himachal Pradesh, were included. 
• **Low population density:** Low-density areas often face higher costs in providing basic services. 
• **Strategic location:** Many SCS states are located on international borders, requiring additional security and development measures. 
• **Economic backwardness:** Poor infrastructure and lack of industrial development were key considerations. 
• **Non-viable nature of state finances:** These states often had lower revenue generation capacity and higher dependency on central assistance. 
• **Benefits of Special Category Status:** 
• **Central Assistance:** SCS states received **90% of funds as grants** and only **10% as loans** under central schemes. 
• **Tax Concessions:** Industries in SCS states were provided tax incentives to promote development. 
• **Preferential Allocation:** SCS states were prioritized for funding under centrally sponsored schemes. 
• **States with Special Category Status:** 
• Initially, the status was granted to **Assam, Nagaland, Jammu & Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh**. 
• Later, states like **Manipur, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Tripura, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand** were added. 
• **14th Finance Commission Recommendations:** 
• The 14th Finance Commission recommended discontinuing the SCS distinction. 
• Instead, it suggested transferring a greater share of central taxes to all states (42% from the divisible pool). 
• However, some benefits of SCS status, like tax incentives, are still provided through **central legislation**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Difference between Special Category Status and Special Status:** 
• **Special Category Status:** Administrative classification granted by the NDC for central assistance based on specific criteria. 
• **Special Status:** Constitutional provision under **Article 371** to provide certain privileges and autonomy to specific states. 
• **Recent Developments:** 
• The **reorganization of Jammu & Kashmir** in 2019 led to the abrogation of its SCS privileges. 
• States like Andhra Pradesh continue to demand SCS status due to financial constraints post-bifurcation. </ul
